Learning Objectives
Describe the common infecting organisms responsible for musculoskeletal infection and their
clinical presentation in various anatomic sites.

management of musculoskeletal infection.

Musculoskeletal Infection: Epidemiology and Microbiology
S aureus is responsible for most musculoskeletal infections, followed by Staphylococcus
epidermidis and related coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species.1 Enterococcus species
and E coli are less prevalent. Anaerobes are uncommon, with the exception of
Cutibacterium acnes, an aerotolerant anaerobic, gram-positive bacterium. Differences in
genetic strain, virulence, and antibiotic resistance patterns are demonstrable between
community-acquired MRSA and hospital-acquired MRSA. Hospital-acquired strains have
broader antibiotic resistance, and community-acquired strains are more likely to carry
Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL)-encoding genes.2 S aureus, Streptococcus species, and
N gonorrhoeae show a high affinity for synovium. Conversely, facultative anaerobic gram-
negative bacilli, such as E coli, rarely infect synovium. With septic arthritis, pathogens
vary with patient age. With the exception of children younger than 4 years, S aureus is
the most frequent pathogen found among all ages and risk categories in the setting of
septic arthritis. Streptococcus species are the next most common pathogens in adults,
and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) is isolated most often. In contrast to septic arthritis
in adults, group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) has a predilection for two
groups: neonates and infirm, elderly patients, particularly those with diabetes mellitus.
Group D Streptococcus species have been reclassified as Enterococcus species, which
uncommonly cause septic arthritis.
Gram-negative cocci less commonly cause septic arthritis, comprising approximately
20% of cases. N gonorrhoeae and N meningitidis are the most commonly isolated gram-
negative species. N gonorrhoeae is the most frequent causative organism of septic knee
arthritis in young, sexually active patients. Gonococcal arthritis , also referred to as
arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, manifests as a bacteremic infection, in 60% of patients or
as a localized septic arthritis in 40% of patients. Arthritis-dermatitis syndrome includes
the triad of dermatitis, tenosynovitis, and migratory or additive polyarthritis. Skin lesions,
found in 75% of patients, are small erythematous papules that may progress to pustules.
Urethral specimens demonstrating polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocytes with
intracellular gram-negative diplococci are diagnostic for infection with N gonorrhoeae in
symptomatic men. N meningitides is underestimated as a cause of septic arthritis.
Concomitant septic arthritis occurs in 2% to 12% of patients with meningococcemia.

Gram-negative bacilli account for 10% to 20% of septic arthritis. Some common
pathogens include E coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter. These organisms most
often affect neonates, intravenous drug abusers, and elderly immunocompromised
patients with diabetes mellitus. S aureus is the most common infectious agent in
intravenous drug users; however, such patients also are highly susceptible to
Pseudomonas, S epidermidis, Serratia, mixed bacterial, and fungal infections.
Another gram-negative organism with unique characteristics in septic arthritis is K
kingae, a slow-growing gram-negative coccobacillus normally colonizing the oropharynx
in 12% of 2-year-old children. It causes infection in children aged 6 months to 4 years
and is the single most common bacterial cause of osteoarticular infections in children
younger than 4 years, causing far more cases of septic arthritis than osteomyelitis.
Colonized children are far more prone to osteoarticular infection. The clinical
presentation is subtle and may be associated with few systemic symptoms and normal
levels of acute-phase reactants. Gram stains of joint aspirates often fail to reveal K
kingae, and the organism is difficult to grow on standard media. To consistently identify
the organism, synovial fluid can be placed into blood culture media. In addition, empiric
selection of clindamycin for the treatment of young children with acute hematogenous
osteomyelitis (AHO) would cover most gram-positive organisms but offers no activity
against K kingae. For decades, H influenzae was the predominant cause of septic arthritis
in children younger than 3 years. Since the advent of the H influenzae type B vaccine, this
pathogen has been superseded by K kingae.
In contrast to septic arthritis, the most common cause of osteomyelitis across all age
groups is S aureus (Table 2). In osteomyelitis, antibiotic resistance correlates with
treatment outcomes, and complication rates of community-acquired MRSA are
associated with a longer treatment course and an increased risk of subperiosteal and
deep abscess formation, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and septic pulmonary emboli
compared with methicillin-sensitive S aureus (MSSA). An important pathogen in
osteomyelitis in specific patient populations is Salmonellae. It is most the prevalent form
of bacterial osteomyelitis in patients with sickling hemoglobinopathies in the United
States. In shoulder surgery, the most common pathogen that causes deep infection is C
acnes, a slow-growing, facultative anaerobic, gram-positive rod. C acnes is the most
common pathogen in periprosthetic shoulder infection. Another noteworthy issue is the

The clinical presentation of musculoskeletal infection varies based on patient age, chronicity,
virulence, variability among bacterial strains, biofilm formation, host viability and immune
status, site, previous management, and circulation.

Musculoskeletal Infections in Adults
The risk factors for septic arthritis are listed in Table 3. Septic arthritis most often is
monoarticular. The knee is affected in 50% of patients, followed by, in decreasing order,
the hip, shoulder, and elbow. Unusual locations, such as the sacroiliac and
sternoclavicular joints, are affected more often in parenteral drug users. Symptoms
suggestive of systemic infection may be lacking. Only 60% of patients are febrile on
presentation. Adult osteomyelitis frequently is associated with posttraumatic, implant-
associated conditions or contiguous spread from adjacent soft-tissue infection, such as
in DFI. Osteomyelitis is classified by its chronicity (acute, subacute, chronic) and
mechanism of infection (hematogenous versus nonhematogenous). Among the most
common causes of osteomyelitis in adults is implant-associated infection, which may
affect many sites, including the articular spaces in the setting of joint replacement and
extra-articular locations in the setting of trauma or reconstructive surgery of the spine,

S aureus is the most common organism found in implant-associated infection, noted in
as many as 50% of patients. Other common organisms include S epidermidis, coagulase-
negative Staphylococcal species, and Streptococcal species. C acnes is the organism most
isolated in as many as 50% of prosthetic shoulder infections. It is a normal part of the
microbiota of the skin and the mucosal surfaces, residing primarily in sebaceous glands
and hair follicles. Spine infections are another example of implant-associated infection
and hematogenous osteomyelitis. The overall incidence of spinal infections is
approximately 2.2 per 100,000 individuals per year, and the postoperative occurrence
rate of spine infections is between 0.3% and 20%. The lumbar spine is the most frequent
site of infection (58%), followed by the thoracic spine (30%) and the cervical spine (11%).6
DFI typically leads to osteomyelitis from contiguous soft-tissue ulceration and spreads
from adjacent tissue. It is one of the most common causes of nonhematogenous
osteomyelitis in adults. DFI typically is a polymicrobial infection of a diabetic foot ulcer
that spreads contiguously to the underlying bone. Patients with DFI have the highest
mortality risk, with a reported 5-year mortality rate of 50%.3-5 In addition, two-thirds of
lower extremity amputations are associated with DFI.4,5S aureus is the organism most
frequently isolated from DFI, with a prevalence rate of 50%. Other organisms, such as S
epidermidis, Streptococcus agalactiae, and Enterococcus, also have been isolated from

tract, a rare complication is the development of malignant squamous cell carcinoma
transformation. Degeneration develops in patients with long-standing osteomyelitis,
usually 20 to 40 years into the disease. The onset of new bleeding or other changes in a
sinus tract warrant biopsy. A radical surgical approach is advised for the management of
squamous cell carcinoma arising within a sinus tract.

Septic arthritis
Early diagnosis is important because extensive cartilage damage can develop within hours.
Neonates and infants with septic arthritis present a more deceptive clinical picture than
older children. Features such as irritability and failure to thrive are nonspecific.
In infants, septic arthritis of the hip produces a flexed, abducted, externally rotated position
to accommodate increased joint volume.
Transient synovitis is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children aged 3 to 10
years. A clinical prediction rule based on four independent factors for hip septic arthritis has
been validated.
History of fever
Refusal to bear weight
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) higher than 40 mm/h
Peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count higher than 12,000 cells/μL
Diagnostic accuracy ranges from 73% to 93% if three predictors are present.
Additionally, a C-reactive protein (CRP) level higher than 2 mg/dL (20 mg/L) is a fifth factor
found in a subsequent study, in which an temperature higher than 101.3°F (38.5°C) and a
CRP level higher than 2 mg/dL (20 mg/L) were found to be most predictive.
In order of highest predictive value: fever > CRP level > ESR > refusal to bear weight > WBC

Peripheral WBC count higher than 12,000 cells/μL
CRP level higher than 13 mg/L

Musculoskeletal Infections in Children
Septic arthritis is one of the most common orthopaedic infections in children. Early
diagnosis is critical, because the consequences of delayed diagnosis are profound;
extensive cartilage damage may develop within hours. Neonates and infants with septic
arthritis present a more deceptive clinical picture than children, and a high index of
suspicion for additional workup is necessary. Features such as irritability and failure to
thrive are nonspecific. In infants, septic arthritis of the hip produces a flexed, abducted,
externally rotated position to accommodate increased joint volume. Inflammatory
conditions in children may mimic the clinical presentation of septic arthritis. For
example, transient synovitis is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children
aged 3 to 10 years. The distinction between septic arthritis and transient synovitis is a
challenge in a child with an acutely irritable hip. A clinical prediction rule based on four
independent factors for hip septic arthritis has been validated: (1) history of fever, (2)
refusal to bear weight, (3) ESR higher than 40 mm/h, and (4) peripheral WBC count
greater than 12,000 cells/μL. The diagnostic accuracy ranges from 73% to 93% if three
predictors are present. Importantly, the rule does not reliably distinguish K kingae septic
arthritis from transient synovitis.
Osteomyelitis is another common cause of musculoskeletal infection in children. It is
most commonly hematogenous or spread from an adjacent septic arthritis. S aureus is
the most common pathogen found in pediatric AHO. An algorithm for distinguishing
MRSA from MSSA osteomyelitis in children has identified four important independent
multivariate predictors: (1) temperature higher than 100.4°F (38°C), (2) hematocrit level
less than 34%, (3) peripheral WBC count higher than 12,000 cells/μL, and (4) CRP level
higher than 13 mg/L. The probability of MRSA osteomyelitis is 92% for all four predictors,
45% for three predictors, 10% for two predictors, 1% for one predictor, and zero for no
predictors. Hematogenous osteomyelitis is far more common in children than adults.
The initial site of infection is metaphyseal, owing to an abundant vascular supply and the
presence of large sinusoids at the epiphyseal-metaphyseal junction. The physis serves a
protective function, impeding infection from entering the epiphysis and (in nonarticular
physes) the joint until physeal closure. In the proximal femur, proximal humerus, distal
lateral tibia, distal fibula, and proximal radius, the metaphysis is intracapsular. In these
joints, hematogenous osteomyelitis may decompress directly into the articulation.

Biofilm Infections
The pathogenesis of musculoskeletal infection typically involves distinct steps of
inoculation of the infecting organism, immune system evasion, and establishment of a
biofilm. Anatomic properties of the joint capsule make it more susceptible to deep
infection. The synovium has no limiting basement membrane, allowing microorganisms
to more readily enter the synovial fluid. The risk of SSI increases if a surgical site is
contaminated with more than 105 microorganisms per gram of tissue. The size of the
inoculum may be considerably smaller in the presence of foreign material, such as
sutures or implants. Infection of the bone presents a unique set of immune challenges
because of the different modes of its colonization and persistence within the bone.7,8
Abscess formation involves S aureus hijacking host-induced processes to create a
protective abscess with bacterial cells at its core that are inaccessible to immune cell
infiltration. Several proteins, such as clumping factor A, staphylococcal complement
inhibitor, and chemotaxis inhibitory protein of staphylococci, are involved in abscess
formation. Abscesses infected with Staphylococcus in patients with osteomyelitis usually
form in the bone marrow space and adjacent soft tissues.7,9 Osteocyte lacuna-
canalicular network invasion refers to the invasion of the submicron channels deep
within the cortical bone. Buried within the dense mineral matrix of bone are osteocytes,
which are interconnected through canaliculi containing their cell processes.10,11
Intracellular colonization of nonprofessional phagocytes, such as osteoblasts,
osteoclasts, and osteocytes, may provide S aureus with a mechanism of immune cell
evasion and protection from antibiotic management. Biofilms formed on implanted
materials and necrotic bone are the most recognized forms of S aureus persistence in
patients with osteomyelitis.
Biofilms are formed over time as an adaptive response to hostile environments, allowing
single-celled organisms to survive in a multicellular community.12 A biofilm is a
community of bacterial cells (15%) embedded in a self-generated protein-polysaccharide
complex (85%) referred to as an extracellular polymeric substance (Figure 1). S aureus

uses a number of virulence factors that assist in its evasion of host immunity, including
the secretion of protein A, which inactivates immunoglobulin G antibodies. The
production of a capsular polysaccharide, which reduces opsonization and phagocytosis,
is another important mechanism of action. PVL is a cytotoxin that lyses WBCs and causes

The formation of a biofilm is among the most challenging aspects of the management of
musculoskeletal infection. Most bacterial infections are caused by organisms growing in
biofilms. The formation of adherent, multilayered biofilms is central to the pathogenesis
of medical device–associated infections. Biofilms may form in a matter of hours after
inoculation.12 Biofilm formation proceeds in four generalized steps, including (1)
bacterial cell attachment to a surface, (2) cell proliferation, (3) biofilm maturation, and (4)
detachment and dispersal. A biofilm strongly adheres to an inert or biologic surface. The
biofilm is remarkably resistant to shear and, therefore, difficult to dislodge. Because
extracellular polymeric substance is not water soluble, irrigation is inadequate to remove
a biofilm. Bacterial sensitivity does not reflect the ability of an antibiotic agent to
eradicate microbes growing in a biofilm. Bacteria in biofilms may display resistance to

Antibiotic Prophylaxis
Routine antibiotic prophylaxis currently is not recommended for elective orthopaedic surgery
that does not involve a prosthetic device.
Timing of antibiotic prophylaxis
Prophylactic intravenous antibiotic agents should be administered within 1 hour of skin
incision. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends achieving
bactericidal tissue concentrations before proceeding.
Because of its extended infusion time, vancomycin should be initiated within 2 hours of skin
incision.
Additional antibiotic doses are administered if surgical time exceeds one to two times the
antibiotic half-life or if substantial blood loss occurs.
Duration of prophylactic antibiotic administration should not exceed the 24-hour
postoperative period.
Updated CDC guidelines suggest only a single dose of prophylactic antibiotic agents, in
contrast to previous guidelines, which recommended 24-hour administration.32

than one-half of orthopaedic SSIs are caused by S aureus, which is carried in the nares
of as many as 30% of patients. In fact, 85% of SSIs caused by S aureus involve strains
found in patients’ own nares. Higher rates of SSI are found in patients colonized with
MRSA. Just less than 1% of the population carries MRSA. Preoperative skin preparation
via chlorhexidine wipes before knee and hip arthroplasty has been shown to reduce
SSI. Nasal sterilization of patients colonized with MRSA/MSSA may be warranted.
Controversies regarding preoperative decolonization include whether to perform
universal decolonization or use selective screening to identify carriers; the method of
decolonization: mupirocin, topical agents such as chlorhexidine 5% with or without
povidone-iodine, or whole-body decolonization versus just the nares; the cost
effectiveness of various protocols; concerns about the creation of resistant organisms;
and addressing persistent colonization shortly after decolonization protocols.40
Obesity is a risk factor for SSI in many types of orthopaedic surgery. However, obesity
as a modifiable risk factor before elective surgery remains controversial. Mixed
reports have surfaced regarding the role of bariatric surgery before joint replacement
to reduce SSI risk, with some studies suggesting advantages and other studies

Another risk factor for SSI found in many studies is malnutrition, which is common in
elderly patients irrespective of body habitus. Markers of malnutrition include a serum
albumin level less than 3.5 mg/dL, a serum transferrin level less than 200 mg/dL, and
a total lymphocyte count less than 1,500/mm3. Malnutrition may be a modifiable risk
factor before elective surgery. A study providing a nutritional intervention program
consisting of a high-protein and anti-inflammatory diet for patients with preoperative
hypoalbuminemia before joint arthroplasty reported reduced readmissions and
hospital lengths of stay in the intervention group.43
Tobacco use increases SSI risk. Tobacco abstinence for at least 30 days before elective
surgery has been advocated. Smoking cessation programs, consisting of counseling,
nicotine substitutes, and referrals to outpatient programs if necessary, may be a cost-
effective intervention to reduce SSI rates and may lead to longer-term behavioral
modifications.44,45
Dentition also may affect SSI rates. Bacteremia associated with dental pathology may
lead to postoperative joint infection in patients undergoing TJA, in the postoperative
interval and subsequently. The prevalence of unmanaged dental conditions in
arthroplasty candidates is disturbingly high. Dental evaluation for gingivitis, decay,
and abscess should be performed before TJA. The 2012 American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons/American Dental Association Evidence-Based Clinical Practice
Guideline on the Prevention of Orthopaedic Implant Infection in Patients Undergoing
Dental Procedures states that the evidence for dental prophylaxis before joint
replacement remains limited. Good evidence is available to suggest that dental
prophylaxis reduces bacteremia; however, the evidence for the connection between
bacteremia and subsequent joint infection is limited (Resource 3). Prophylaxis is not
recommended for implants in extra-synovial locations, such as fracture plates.

Perioperative urinary tract infection also may affect SSI rates. Preoperative urinalysis
and urine culture may be indicated in patients with urinary tract symptoms and those
at greater risk for urinary tract infection. Indications to consider postponing surgery
include dysuria and frequency in patients with a colony count higher than 103
CFU/mL. No reason exists for diagnosing or managing asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis who undergo TJA have a two to three times higher
risk of SSI than patients with osteoarthritis. Other immunocompromised patients also
have an increased risk (Table 7). The use of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs in
the perioperative period may increase the rate of SSI, and management criteria have
been established to help guide their use. In 2017, the American College of
Rheumatology and the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons created
guidelines for the perioperative management of disease-modifying agents before
elective hip and knee replacement.36 Methotrexate, sulfasalazine,
hydroxychloroquine, and leflunomide can be continued throughout the perioperative
period.
Increased SSI rates are a known complication of biologic agents, such as anti-TNF
agents (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab), other targeted biologic therapies
(rituximab, anakinra, tofacitinib), and other immunosuppressive agents (cyclosporine,
tacrolimus, azathioprine). In patients undergoing major surgery, these agents should
be withheld preoperatively for at least one dosing cycle (depending on the half-life of
the drug) and postoperatively until wound healing is ensured.
Corticosteroids increase the infection rate and impair wound healing. Keeping the
dose as low as possible can be attempted to decrease SSI rates. Patients taking 5 mg
or less of prednisone equivalents per day or patients with less than 3 weeks of
corticosteroid treatment do not need stress dose steroids in the perioperative period.
If a patient takes 20 mg or more per day for more than 3 weeks, then stress dose
steroids are recommended. Postoperative adrenal crisis may mimic other acute
postoperative conditions, such as infection, and includes symptoms such as refractory
hypotension, fever, altered mental status, and tachycardia.

Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis is the only treatment option that qualifies as a
standard of care in patients with an implant. CDC guidelines on the prevention of SSI
from 1999 and updates in 2014 recommend a single dose of perioperative antibiotic
agents in any surgical procedure that entails incision through normal tissue with no
existing inflammation or infection but involves the placement of an extravascular
prosthetic material or in which a deep infection poses catastrophic risk. This
recommendations covers many orthopaedic surgical procedures.37,38 Alcohol-based
solutions with iodophor or chlorhexidine appear to be the most effective antiseptic
agents. Chlorhexidine may be more effective against gram-positive organisms than
aqueous-based iodophors, such as povidone-iodine. Chlorhexidine has residual
antimicrobial properties because of its ability to bind to skin. It is less likely to be
inactivated by blood or serum proteins than the iodophors.
Gloves are uniformly punctured after 3 hours of surgery; therefore, double gloving is
highly recommended. Among absorbable synthetic sutures, monofilament is
associated with a lower risk of infection than braided material. Both are superior to
nonabsorbable braided or natural sutures. Occlusive dressings are associated with a
lower rate of infection. Retention of postsurgical drains for more than 24 hours is
associated with an increased risk of contamination from resistant nosocomial
organisms. However, extended antibiotic agents in patients with a drain are not
recommended. Surgical duration longer than 2 hours is an independent risk factor for
SSI. Hypothermia during surgery is an independent risk factor for SSI.
Postoperative hyperglycemia is an independent risk factor for SSI. Diabetes mellitus
and morning postoperative hyperglycemia are predictors for postoperative infection
after TJA. Perioperative glycemic control, with a target serum glucose level less than
200 mg/dL and preferably less than 140 mg/dL, is strongly advocated by the CDC for
patients with or without diabetes mellitus.34 Prolonged wound drainage exceeding 5
postoperative days is correlated with an increased risk of deep SSI. Allogeneic blood
transfusion may be an overlooked risk factor for postoperative bacterial infection.
Each unit of intraoperative or postoperative allogeneic blood may increase the risk of
SSI by as much as 9%. TXA is an antifibrinolytic agent that is a synthetic analog of
lysine. The use of TXA intravenously, topically, or orally in the perioperative period
multiple types of orthopaedic surgical procedures has resulted in reduced rates of
